title: Z + narzędnik
note: Second job of the instrumental, straight off a1_inst_job: same case, same endings (-em / -ą), new duty — companionship after z. The unit is deliberately ONE new thing: the preposition z now governs the instrumental. Twelve nouns, twelve forms, and every stage carries all twelve, so match/quiz/type/use are the same paradigm at four depths (stage overlap is allowed, James 2026-08-05). Six masculine-side / six feminine to keep the board balanced. FENCED: plural instrumental (z rodzicami, z dziećmi) — B1, different ending set; transport uses (jadę autobusem) — later unit; z mężem (mąż has an ą→ę stem shift, not worth an exception here); z przyjacielem (soft -iel declension). Forks taken, conservative path per batch rule 7: (a) kim is a new pronoun form and is not in POOL, so it is never taught, never glossed in English and never demanded by a prompt — it appears only in the mandated title and, mirroring it, in the Polish shorthand line of two intro slides, exactly as other packs use untaught grammar metalanguage there (miejscownik, dopełniacz). If James wants Z kim? as a live question it needs its own small unit; (b) the z+Gen vs z+Inst contrast is stated once in intro slide 4 but never drilled as its own quiz stem — instead the genitive forms sit inside the quiz distractors (z brata, z taty, z babci), which gets the discrimination without rebuilding the old do/z cliff. dzieckiem is recycled in the endings table only (already taught in a1_inst_job) and is never demanded by a prompt.

intro.title: Saying who you are with
intro.body:
English puts the person straight after with — with my brother, with mum.

Polish uses z, and the person's name changes its ending. The case is the instrumental (narzędnik) — the very one you already used for jobs in Jestem nauczycielem.

brat → z bratem
mama → z mamą

Nothing else in the sentence moves.

One thing to expect: Polish normally leaves mój out. z bratem on its own already means with my brother. (mój would change shape after z as well — that is a later lesson.)
intro.body_pl: z + narzędnik = z kim. Ta sama końcówka co w Jestem nauczycielem. mój zwykle pomijamy.

intro.title: The endings — you already have them
intro.body:
Read this table twice: it is the same table as Jestem studentem / Jestem lekarką. Same case, new job — there it said who somebody is, here it says who you are with.

Watch the second row. tata and kolega end in -a and look feminine, but they are masculine. Luckily the ending follows the look, not the gender: they take -ą, exactly like mama.
intro.body_pl: m. -em · m. na -a → -ą · ż. -ą · n. -em (znane z dzieckiem).

rows: brat → z bratem · syn → z synem
tata → z tatą · kolega → z kolegą
mama → z mamą · żona → z żoną

intro.title: Two nouns that shift: wujek, dziadek
intro.body:
Nouns ending in -ek drop that e the moment any ending is added. The k that is left then takes -iem, not plain -em.

Both things happen in one step, so learn the finished form whole.

The i is the same fact you met in banki and książki: after k, Polish reaches for i. Feminine -ka words are safe — the ending there is -ą, and córką, kuzynką, wnuczką need no i at all.
intro.body_pl: -ek: e wypada, k + iem. Rodzaj żeński na -ka bez zmian: córką.

intro.title: z has two jobs
intro.body:
You already know a z: the one meaning from. z domu = from home. That z takes the genitive.

This unit is the other z: with. That one takes the instrumental. Same little word, two jobs — and the ending on the noun is what tells them apart.
intro.body_pl: z + dopełniacz = skąd. z + narzędnik = z kim.

examples.en: I'm going to the park with my brother.
Dad was drinking coffee with my uncle.

quiz.explain: z brata would be the genitive — the z that means from. Companionship needs the instrumental, so the masculine ending is -em.
Two changes at once: the e of wujek falls out, and the k left behind takes -iem rather than -em.
dziadek behaves exactly like wujek — the e goes, and k pulls in the i. It is a pattern, not a one-off.
kolega is masculine but ends in -a, and the ending follows the shape of the word: -ą, like mama. Only nouns ending in a consonant take -em.
Same trap as kolega. tata is a man, but the word ends in -a, so the ending is -ą. You still say mój tata — the gender shows up there, not here.
No i is needed here. The k only asks for one in front of e — and this ending is -ą, so córka simply becomes córką.
babcia already carries an i before its -a. Swap the a for ą and the i stays where it was: babcią.

type_items.explain: Two words only. Polish leaves mój out here — z bratem already carries with my brother.
wujek loses its e before any ending, then the k takes -iem.
A word ending in -a takes -ą, whether it is a man or a woman. tata is the classic case.
